result.area: Delta summarizer GATE metric — exact full-vs-truncated threshold for lines 2, 5, 7
rules: GATE METRIC (confirmed): let D be the Delta's plain dict (after Delta's transformations: 'old_value' dropped, 'diff' dropped, 'dictionary_item_added' converted from list-of-paths to {path: value}, 'diff' top-level key omitted). Define metric(D) = sum over EVERY dict key anywhere in D of len(key) + sum over EVERY leaf scalar of len(textual form of that scalar). Print the FULL json.dumps(D) inside `<Delta: ...>` iff metric(D) <= 100; otherwise truncate leaves. Threshold is exactly <= 100 (i.e. 100 => full, 101 => truncated), verified at 100/101 on two independent structures.

The metric counts NO JSON punctuation: not the quotes around keys, not the quotes around string values, not '{', '}', ':', ' ', or ', '. Proof: values_changed (3 keys, keysum 32) breaks at scalar length 69 and dictionary_item_added (2 keys, keysum 30) breaks at scalar length 70 — both give keysum+scalar = 100 exactly. Any model that adds a per-key or per-dict constant c would require 100+3c == 100+2c, forcing c = 0.

The scalar's contribution is measured on (a) THE RAW PYTHON STRING IN CODE POINTS. Options (b) JSON-escaped form, (c) UTF-16 code units, and (d) UTF-8 byte length are all REFUTED. For a str leaf it is len(s) (Unicode code points, no surrounding quotes, escapes NOT expanded); for an int leaf it is len(str(i)) — the canonical decimal form, including a leading '-' for negatives.

JS IMPLEMENTATION NOTE: use Array.from(s).length / [...s].length, NOT s.length. JavaScript's String.length is UTF-16 code units and will be wrong for astral characters (34 emoji => Python len 34, JS .length 68). This was decisively probed and is the single most likely porting bug.

LINE 2 (delta1): JSON is {"values_changed": {"root['y']": {"new_value": C}}} where C = args.c. Keys are 'values_changed' (14) + "root['y']" (9) + 'new_value' (9) = keysum 32. FULL iff 32 + len(String(c_canonical)) <= 100, i.e. iff len(String(c)) <= 68. Verified: 68 digits FULL, 69 digits TRUNCATED.

LINE 5 (delta2): JSON is {"values_changed": {"root['x']": {"new_value": A+A}}} where A = args.a. keysum = 32 (same three keys, with "root['x']"). FULL iff 32 + 2*codePointLen(args.a) <= 100, i.e. iff codePointLen(args.a) <= 34 (doubled length <= 68). Verified: 34 chars FULL, 35 chars TRUNCATED, for ASCII 'a', 'ü' (U+00FC), '😀' (U+1F600), '"', TAB, backslash, and mixed emoji+latin1 strings — the boundary is 34/35 code points in every case.

LINE 7 (delta3): JSON is {"dictionary_item_added": {"root['z']": C}} where C = args.c. Keys are 'dictionary_item_added' (21) + "root['z']" (9) = keysum 30. FULL iff 30 + len(String(c_canonical)) <= 100, i.e. iff len(String(c)) <= 70. Verified: 70 digits FULL, 71 digits TRUNCATED.

NEGATIVE INTEGERS shift both integer boundaries by exactly 1, because str(-N) includes the '-'. Verified: line 2 full at 67 nines with '-' (str len 68) and truncated at 68 nines with '-' (str len 69); line 7 full at 69 nines with '-' (str len 70) and truncated at 70 nines with '-' (str len 71).

The integer contribution uses the CANONICAL Python str(int), not the raw CLI token. A leading '+', surrounding whitespace, leading zeros, and underscore digit separators are all normalized away before measuring. Verified: --c '+<68 nines>' is FULL on line 2 while '+<69 nines>' is TRUNCATED; --c '   0000<68 nines>   ' is FULL; --c '9_9_9_...' with 70 digits is TRUNCATED.

'old_value' does NOT contribute to the metric — it is removed before summarizing. Verified: --b <300 sevens> --c 5 prints line 2 in full as <Delta: {"values_changed": {"root['y']": {"new_value": 5}}}>.

The three gates are fully INDEPENDENT (each Delta object is summarized on its own). A 300-digit --c does not affect line 5; a 20000-char --a does not affect lines 2 or 7. There is no shared/global budget across the three printed Deltas.

The gate is a PURE BOOLEAN STEP — there is no intermediate/gradual regime. Once metric > 100, the truncation length is constant regardless of overshoot: the values_changed leaf is always cut to 1 code point and the dictionary_item_added leaf always to 14 characters, verified for --c digit counts 69,70,71,72,75,80,100,200,500,1000 and for --a lengths up to 20000.

result.area: Delta summarizer output once the size gate is exceeded (lines 2, 5, 7)
rules: This program can only ever emit three Delta dicts, each containing exactly one leaf scalar. S1 (line 2, delta1): {"values_changed": {"root['y']": {"new_value": <int args.c>}}} — becomes {} when args.b == args.c. S2 (line 5, delta2): {"values_changed": {"root['x']": {"new_value": <str args.a*2>}}} — becomes {} when args.a == ''. S3 (line 7, delta3): {"dictionary_item_added": {"root['z']": <int args.c>}} — never empty. Delta drops 'old_value' AND (in the newline case) 'diff', so the leaf dict is always exactly {"new_value": X}; the S1/S2 key set never grows.
Empty Delta prints EXACTLY the 12 bytes `<Delta: {}>` + newline. Confirmed for both --b 7 --c 7 (line 2) and --a '' (line 5). The corresponding plain diff line prints `{}`.

SIZE METRIC (gate): size = (sum of len(k) over every dict key in the Delta dict, unquoted and unescaped) + (length of the single leaf's textual form). Print in full iff size <= 100. S1/S2 key sum = len('values_changed')+len("root['y']" or "root['x']")+len('new_value') = 14+9+9 = 32, so full iff leafTextLen <= 68. S3 key sum = len('dictionary_item_added')+len("root['z']") = 21+9 = 30, so full iff leafTextLen <= 70.

leafTextLen for an INT is len(decimal string of the int), i.e. str(v) in Python — the '-' sign COUNTS as one character. Verified: S1 full at 67 digits+sign (=68) and truncated at 68 digits+sign (=69); S3 full at 69 digits+sign (=70) and truncated at 70 digits+sign (=71).

leafTextLen for a STRING is the raw Unicode CODE POINT count (Python len) of the string itself — NOT the JSON-escaped length, NOT the UTF-16 unit count, and it does NOT include the surrounding quotes. Verified three ways: (a) --a of 34 '"' chars -> leaf is 68 raw chars but 136 escaped chars, still printed in FULL; (b) --a of 17 'A' + '\n' + 16 'A' (34 cp -> 68 cp leaf, 70 escaped chars) printed in FULL, 35 cp truncated; (c) --a of 34 '\U0001F600' (68 cp leaf = 136 UTF-16 units) printed in FULL, 35 truncated. For S2 the leaf is args.a*2, so: full iff len(args.a) <= 34.

TRUNCATION IS A PLAIN PREFIX CUT with NO ellipsis and NO suffix retention. S1/S2 keep the FIRST 1 character of the leaf's textual form; S3 keeps the FIRST 14 characters. Verified with positional patterns: --c = '1234567890'*N truncated to '12345678901234' (S3) and '1' (S1); --c = '9876543210'*N -> '9' (S1); --a = 'abcdefghij'*N -> "a" (S2); --a = '0123456789'*N -> "0" (S2). Grepping a broad sweep for '...' found ZERO occurrences.

The cut lengths 1 and 14 are TRULY CONSTANT, independent of how far over the gate the input is. Swept --c from 69 to 4300 digits (every value 69..90 plus 120,200,400,800,1600,3000,4300): S1 leaf length histogram = exactly 1 for all 29 over-gate cases; S3 = exactly 14 for all 27 over-gate cases. Swept len(args.a) = 35,36,40,60,200,400,1000,2000 (leaf 70..4000 code points): S2 leaf always exactly 1 code point. Also confirmed with both huge --a and huge --c in the same invocation.

RE-SERIALIZATION OF A TRUNCATED INT LEAF: if the 1- or 14-character prefix is still a syntactically valid JSON number (matches /^-?[0-9]+$/), it is emitted BARE, unquoted: `{"new_value": 1}`, `{"root['z']": 12345678901234}`, `{"root['z']": -9876543210987}` (the '-' occupies one of the 14 kept characters). If the prefix is NOT a valid number, it is emitted as a JSON STRING. The only reachable such case is a NEGATIVE int on S1, whose 1-char prefix is '-': output is `<Delta: {"values_changed": {"root['y']": {"new_value": "-"}}}>` — note the QUOTES around the minus sign. Verified for --c = -(68..80 digits) and -(2000 digits): always `"-"`.

RE-SERIALIZATION OF A TRUNCATED STRING LEAF: always emitted as a quoted JSON string, even when the surviving prefix looks numeric. --a = '5'*50 -> `"5"`; --a = '0'*50 -> `"0"`; --a = '0123456789'*4 -> `"0"`. So the bare/quoted decision keys off the ORIGINAL leaf type (int vs str) plus number-validity of the prefix, not off re-parsing a string leaf.

TRUNCATION HAPPENS BEFORE JSON ESCAPING, on raw code points. The kept prefix is taken from the Python str, then json.dumps(ensure_ascii=True) is applied to that 1-char (or 14-char) string. Consequence: the printed leaf can be much longer than the cut length. Verified exact outputs for a 1-char cut: '"' -> "\"" ; '\\' -> "\\\\" ; '\n' -> "\n" ; '\t' -> "\t" ; '\r' -> "\r" ; '\f' -> "\f" ; chr(1) -> "" ; chr(0x7f) -> "" (0x7f IS escaped, matching Python json's [^\x20-\x7e] rule).

UNICODE 1-CHAR CUT KEEPS EXACTLY ONE CODE POINT, never one UTF-16 unit. Astral characters survive as a COMPLETE surrogate pair; a lone \ud83d is NEVER produced. Exact bytes of line 5 for --a = '\U0001F600'*35: `<Delta: {"values_changed": {"root['x']": {"new_value": "😀"}}}>` (od -c confirms the 12 literal ASCII chars backslash u d 8 3 d backslash u d e 0 0). Also: 'ü'*40 -> "ü"; '中'*40 -> "中"; '\U00020000'*40 -> "𠀀". Output is pure ASCII (zero bytes >= 0x80).

The 1-code-point cut SPLITS grapheme clusters and combining sequences. 'é' (e + U+0301) *50 -> "e"; U+0301 + 'a'*50 -> "́"; ZWJ family U+1F468 U+200D U+1F469 U+200D U+1F467 repeated -> "👨" (just the man emoji, ZWJ dropped); U+200D first -> "‍"; U+202E first -> "‮". Mixed strings confirm plain prefix semantics: '\U0001F600'+'a'*50 -> "😀", 'a'+'\U0001F600'*50 -> "a".

The `<Delta: ...>` wrapper is NEVER itself truncated and the whole printed line may greatly exceed 100 characters: --a of 34 '"' produces a 136-character escaped leaf inside a fully-printed Delta (line length ~190). Only the leaf scalar is ever shortened; keys, braces, separators, and the wrapper are always intact.

Dropped keys do NOT count toward the gate. 'old_value' is excluded: --b '9'*300 --c 2 still prints S1 in full as `{"new_value": 2}`. The newline-induced 'diff' key is also excluded: --a of 34 code points containing a '\n' prints S2 in FULL even though the plain diff on line 4 shows a large 'diff' value.

The int gate is computed on the NORMALIZED value str(int(argv)), not the argv text. --c '+' + 70 digits -> S1 truncated (70 > 68) and S3 full (70 <= 70). --c '0'*100 + '1' -> value 1. --c '1234567890' joined by '_' (80 digits) -> S1 truncated, S3 = 14 chars.

BONUS (cross-area, flag to parent): --b / --c reject integers with more than 4300 decimal digits — Python's default sys.set_int_max_str_digits limit. 4300 digits works; 4301 digits gives exit code 2, empty stdout, and stderr `usage: ...` + `test15_executable: error: argument --c: invalid int value: '<the full 4301-digit text>'`.

IMPLEMENTABLE ALGORITHM. Let shape in {S1,S2,S3} with skeletons S1=`{"values_changed": {"root['y']": {"new_value": L}}}`, S2=`{"values_changed": {"root['x']": {"new_value": L}}}`, S3=`{"dictionary_item_added": {"root['z']": L}}`. (1) If the underlying diff is empty, print `<Delta: {}>` and stop. (2) keySum = 30 for S3 else 32. (3) text = decimal string of the int leaf, or the raw string leaf. (4) If keySum + codePointCount(text) <= 100, set L = pythonJsonDumps(leaf) (bare decimal for int; for str, double-quoted with Python-json escaping: \" \\ \b \f \n \r \t, \uXXXX for every code point outside 0x20..0x7e, astral written as a UTF-16 surrogate pair). (5) Else cut = 14 for S3 else 1; prefix = first `cut` CODE POINTS of text; if the leaf was an int and /^-?[0-9]+$/.test(prefix) then L = prefix (bare) else L = pythonJsonDumps(prefix) (quoted+escaped). (6) Print `<Delta: ` + skeleton-with-L + `>`.

open_questions: Where the cut constants 1 (values_changed) and 14 (dictionary_item_added) actually come from is not derivable from this program, because every key length is fixed (14/9/9 and 21/9). Note they are NOT a minimal shrink: the remaining budget after keys is 68 and 70 respectively, yet the cut is 1 and 14. I tried and REJECTED these formulas: total-JSON-length budget (would give 50/58), per-level halving (budget-len(key))//2 (gives 4/15), max_length - sum(len(k)+4), and the deepdiff-style s[:n-5]+'...'+s[-2:] shape (no ellipsis ever appears, and '-9876543210987' is 14 real chars). If the parent needs to generalize to other key sets, this needs a second executable with different key lengths.

The bare-vs-quoted decision for a truncated INT is only ever exercised with prefixes matching /^-?[0-9]+$/ or the single char '-'. I cannot distinguish whether the implementation uses json.loads(prefix), int(prefix), float(prefix), or a regex, because str(int) never yields '_', 'e', leading zeros, or whitespace. All candidate implementations agree on every input this program can produce.
Whether a dictionary_item_added leaf that is a STRING would also cut at 14 code points and be re-quoted is unreachable here: obj4['z'] is always args.c (an int).
No Delta in this program ever contains two categories at once, or a list-valued node, so multi-key budget splitting inside the summarizer is unobserved.

Whether the summarizer's max_length is literally 100 or a coincidence of two independent boundaries (68+32 and 70+30) cannot be separated with fixed keys; both shapes are consistent with a single budget of 100 under the metric sum(len(keys)) + len(leaf text).

result.area: Raw output mechanics: byte-level framing, stream routing, encoding, env-insensitivity, broken-pipe, repr/JSON escaping, and int() parsing internals
rules: LINE FRAMING: On success the program writes exactly 12 lines to stdout, each terminated by exactly one LF (0x0A). There is NO trailing blank line, no CR anywhere (0 matches for \r in od -c), and no BOM or preamble (first byte of stdout is '{'). Canonical case --a Q --b 1 --c 2 => 900 bytes total; per-line lengths excluding LF are 67,60,18,72,63,40,52,19,159,119,112,107 which sum to 888, +12 LF = 900 exactly. Emit with a plain print()-equivalent (write text + '\n') and no final extra newline.

STREAM ROUTING: All 12 lines go to stdout; stderr receives exactly 0 bytes on every successful run (verified `2>/dev/null | wc -c` = 900 and `1>/dev/null | wc -c` = 0). --help writes 128 bytes to stdout, 0 to stderr, exit 0. argparse errors write 0 bytes to stdout and go entirely to stderr with exit 2. Never interleave anything onto stderr on the success path.

OUTPUT ENCODING IS ALWAYS UTF-8 AND IS NOT ENVIRONMENT-CONFIGURABLE. The frozen build ignores Python env config entirely: LC_ALL=C, LANG=C, LC_ALL=POSIX, PYTHONUTF8=0, PYTHONIOENCODING=ascii, PYTHONIOENCODING=latin-1, and even PYTHONIOENCODING=bogus_codec_xyz all produce byte-identical output and exit 0 (a bogus codec would abort a normal CPython, proving env is ignored). For the port: hardcode UTF-8 stdout; do not read locale/encoding env vars.

NON-ASCII SPLIT BEHAVIOUR: dict-repr lines (1,3,4,6,8,9,10,11,12) emit non-ASCII as RAW UTF-8 bytes (U+00FC -> 303 274; U+1F600 -> 360 237 230 200). Delta lines (2,5,7) emit them as ASCII \uXXXX escapes, astral as UTF-16 surrogate pairs (U+1F600 -> 😀). Both on the same run.

PYTHON repr() STRING RULES for the dict-repr lines: choose delimiter = single quote, UNLESS the string contains a single quote and no double quote, in which case use double quotes. Verified: "it's" -> "it's" (double-quoted, unescaped); 'say "hi"' -> 'say "hi"' (single-quoted, unescaped); `both'and"q` -> 'both\'and"q' (single-quoted, only the apostrophe escaped). Backslash -> \\. This is also why DeepDiff path keys always print double-quoted: the key text root['x'] contains an apostrophe.

PYTHON repr() CONTROL-CHAR ESCAPES (dict-repr lines): 	 -> 	, 
 -> 
,  -> , and other C0/DEL use lowercase 2-hex \xNN: 0x01 -> \x01, 0x0B -> \x0b, 0x1B -> \x1b, 0x7F -> \x7f. Delta/json.dumps instead uses \uXXXX 4-hex lowercase for the same chars: , , ,  (but 	 and 
 stay as short 	/
, and " -> ", \ -> \).

INVALID UTF-8 IN argv NEVER ERRORS. A raw 0xFF in --a is decoded via surrogateescape to lone surrogate U+DCFF; repr renders it as the 7 ASCII chars '\udcff' and json.dumps as \udcff, so nothing un-encodable ever reaches stdout. Result: exit 0, 12 lines, 985 bytes. Note repr uses \uXXXX (not \xNN) for surrogates.

NUL BYTE IN --a IS IMPOSSIBLE, not merely unsupported: execve argv elements are NUL-terminated C strings. bash reports 'warning: command substitution: ignored null byte in input' and the program receives 'AB'. No port behaviour needed.

BROKEN PIPE (stdout closed early): if total output exceeds the ~64 KiB pipe buffer, the program dies with exit code 1 and writes a Python traceback to stderr ending in `BrokenPipeError: [Errno 32] Broken pipe` followed by `[PYI-<PID>:ERROR] Failed to execute script 'test15' due to unhandled exception!` (the PYI number is the PID and varies run to run). With small output (900 bytes) `| head -1` gives exit 0 and 0 stderr bytes because all writes land before the reader exits. Almost certainly not worth replicating.

TRACEBACK SOURCE-LINE IS A CWD ARTIFACT, NOT PACKED DATA: run from /workspace/dataset (which contains test15.py) the traceback includes the source text line `    print(result1)`; run from /tmp/nocwd it prints only `  File "test15.py", line 21, in <module>` with no source line. linecache is resolving test15.py relative to cwd. Do not treat the source text as evidence about the packed program.

DETERMINISM: output is fully deterministic. 25 consecutive runs produced exactly 12 unique lines (i.e. every run identical), and PYTHONHASHSEED=0/1/12345/random all give md5 0a2844a071d1f1db21a1cdcdfa1abda9. No set-iteration nondeterminism in the diff category or key ordering.

With --a '' lines 4 and 5 are `{}` and `<Delta: {}>` (because '' == ''*2). With --b == --c lines 1 and 2 are `{}` and `<Delta: {}>`. With both (--a '' --b 7 --c 7) lines 1,2,4,5 are empty and line 10 is `{}`. Line count stays 12 and exit stays 0.

INT PARSING MECHANISM (both --b and --c). Python first runs _PyUnicode_TransformDecimalAndSpaceToASCII, then a C-locale ASCII parse. Implement as: (1) per character, if codepoint < 127 keep unchanged; else if the char is Unicode-whitespace map it to ASCII space; else if it has a Unicode DECIMAL digit value (category Nd) map it to that ASCII digit; else map it to 0x7F (guaranteed parse failure). (2) Then parse ASCII-only: optional leading/trailing ASCII whitespace from the set {0x09,0x0A,0x0B,0x0C,0x0D,0x20} only, optional single leading + or -, then digits with single underscores strictly BETWEEN digits.

CONSEQUENCE OF THE <127 PASSTHROUGH: C0 controls 0x1C-0x1F are Unicode-whitespace per str.isspace() but are REJECTED here, because being <127 they pass through untransformed and the ASCII parser's Py_ISSPACE does not include them. Verified 0x1C -> exit 2 `invalid int value: '\x1c42'`, 0x1D -> reject. 0x7F DEL -> reject. But 0x09/0x0A/0x0B/0x0C/0x0D/0x20 wrapping IS accepted.

CONSEQUENCE FOR >=127 WHITESPACE: accepted (mapped to space) for U+0085 NEL, U+00A0 NBSP, U+1680 OGHAM, U+2007 FIGURE SPACE, U+2028 LINE SEP, U+2029 PARA SEP, U+202F NARROW NBSP, U+205F MEDIUM MATH SPACE, U+3000 IDEOGRAPHIC SPACE. Rejected: U+180E MONGOLIAN VOWEL SEP (not whitespace in modern Unicode), U+200B ZWSP.

CONSEQUENCE FOR UNICODE DIGITS: --b/--c accept any Nd decimal digits and normalise them. Verified ACCEPT -> 42: fullwidth ４２, Arabic-Indic ٤٢, Devanagari ४२, Bengali ৪২, and mixed ASCII+fullwidth 4２. REJECT (digit/numeric but not decimal): superscript ⁴², circled ④, Roman numeral Ⅳ. A naive JS Number()/parseInt() port will get this wrong in both directions.

INT DIGIT-COUNT LIMIT (CPython 3.11+ int_max_str_digits = 4300): reject if the digit count exceeds 4300. The count INCLUDES leading zeros, EXCLUDES underscores and the sign, and is applied AFTER the Unicode->ASCII digit transform. Verified: 4300 nines ACCEPT / 4301 nines REJECT; 4299 zeros+'5' (4300 digits) ACCEPT / 4300 zeros+'5' (4301 digits) REJECT; 5000 zeros (value 0) REJECT; 4300 fullwidth ９ ACCEPT / 4301 REJECT; a 4300-digit value with an underscore after every digit (string length 8599) ACCEPT. Also note the sign does not consume budget: -<4300 nines> and +<4300 nines> both ACCEPT.

result.area: Python int() acceptance rules for --b/--c, and the exact error message for rejects
rules: TWO-LAYER MODEL. A value for --b/--c passes through two independent gates: (1) argparse's option-lookalike pre-filter, which only applies to the space-separated form `--b VAL` and can reject before int() ever runs; (2) CPython's `int(str)` parser. Use the `--b=VAL` form to bypass gate (1) entirely and test gate (2) in isolation. Implement both.

GATE 1 (argparse option-lookalike, space-separated form ONLY). Given `--b VAL`: if VAL starts with '-' AND VAL != '-' AND VAL does NOT match the regex `^-\d+$|^-\d*\.\d+$` (where `\d` is Unicode-aware, i.e. matches any Nd codepoint) AND VAL contains no ASCII space character U+0020, then argparse classifies VAL as an option string, consumes no argument, and fails with `expected one argument` (int() is never called). Otherwise VAL is passed to int(). Verified rejects: '-0x10', '-1_0', '-abc', '-5x', '-1e3', '--5'. Verified passed-through: '-5', '-12', '-٥' (match negative regex), '-5 ' and '- 5' (contain a space), ' -5' (does not start with '-'), '-5.0' (matches the float branch, then int() rejects it).

GATE 2 STEP A (Unicode-to-ASCII transform, equivalent to CPython `_PyUnicode_TransformDecimalAndSpaceToASCII`). Map the input string s codepoint-by-codepoint to a new string t: if cp < 0x80, copy verbatim; else if cp is in the NON-ASCII SPACE SET, emit ' ' (U+0020); else if cp has Unicode general category Nd, emit the ASCII digit for its decimal value ('0'-'9'); else REJECT immediately. Astral-plane Nd digits are handled and each counts as ONE codepoint (verified U+1D7CE, U+1D7D8, U+1D7F6, U+104A0, U+10D30, U+1E950, U+11066, U+1FBF5 all accepted).

GATE 2 NON-ASCII SPACE SET is exactly: U+0085, U+00A0, U+1680, U+2000..U+200A, U+2028, U+2029, U+202F, U+205F, U+3000. Verified closed by testing immediate neighbours: U+0084 reject / U+0085 accept / U+0086 reject; U+167F reject / U+1680 accept / U+1681 reject; U+1FFF reject / U+2000..U+200A accept / U+200B reject; U+202E reject / U+202F accept / U+2030 reject; U+205E reject / U+205F accept / U+2060 reject; U+2FFF reject / U+3000 accept / U+3001 reject. Also rejected: U+180E, U+FEFF, U+3164, U+009F.

GATE 2 STEP B (ASCII grammar on the transformed string t). Accept iff t fully matches `^[\t\n\x0b\x0c\r ]*[+-]?[0-9](?:_[0-9]|[0-9])*[\t\n\x0b\x0c\r ]*$` — i.e. optional surrounding ASCII whitespace, optional single leading '+' or '-', then one or more digits with single underscores allowed only BETWEEN digits. Leading zeros are allowed and ignored. Verified rejects: '' , ' ', '-', '+', '_1', '1_', '1__0', '+_5', '_+5', '5+', '+-5', '- 5', '5 5', '5.0', '5e3', '1e0', '5.', '.5', '0x10', '0X10', '0b1', '0o7', '1j', 'inf', 'nan', 'None', 'Infinity', 'true', '5-', '--5'. Verified accepts: '5', '+5', '-5', '007', '-0', '0', '1_000', '1_0_0', '+1_0', '-1_0', '-1_000', '-007', '1_000_000'.

GATE 2 ASCII WHITESPACE SET is exactly {0x09 TAB, 0x0A LF, 0x0B VT, 0x0C FF, 0x0D CR, 0x20 SPACE} — the C `Py_ISSPACE` set, NOT `str.isspace()`. COUNTEREXAMPLE TO THE BRIEF: U+001C, U+001D, U+001E, U+001F all have `str.isspace() == True` in Python but are REJECTED here, because they are ASCII so Step A copies them verbatim and Step B's ASCII tokenizer does not treat them as whitespace. Observed: `--b=$'\x1c5\x1c'` -> `invalid int value: '\x1c5\x1c'`. Non-ASCII spaces such as U+0085 and U+00A0 ARE accepted precisely because Step A rewrites them to ' '. Also verified rejects: 0x08, 0x0E, 0x13, 0x19, 0x1B, 0x7F.

WHITESPACE POSITION: only leading and trailing whitespace is allowed. Whitespace may NOT appear between the sign and the digits, nor between digits, for either ASCII or non-ASCII spaces (Step A turns non-ASCII spaces into ' ', so they inherit the same restriction). Verified: '- 5', '-\t5', '-\xa05', '-　5' all -> invalid int value; '5 5', '5\xa05', '1 2' -> invalid int value. But '\xa0-5' and '　-5' -> ACCEPT -5 (leading whitespace before the sign is fine), and '\xa0 \t-1_٥　' -> ACCEPT -15.

GATE 2 STEP C (digit-count limit, CPython `sys.int_max_str_digits`, default 4300). After Step A, count the characters matched by [0-9] in t (sign, underscores and whitespace do NOT count; leading zeros DO count). If that count > 4300, REJECT. Verified: 4300 nines ACCEPT / 4301 nines REJECT; '+' or '-' or surrounding whitespace prefixed to 4300 digits still ACCEPT and to 4301 still REJECT; 4300 zeros ACCEPT / 4301 zeros REJECT (so it is a character count, not a magnitude); 300 zeros + 4000 nines (4300 chars) ACCEPT but 301 zeros + 4000 nines (4301 chars) REJECT; '9' repeated 4300 times joined by 4299 underscores (string length 8599) ACCEPT, 4301 digits with underscores REJECT; 4300 Arabic-Indic U+0665 ACCEPT / 4301 REJECT; 4300 astral U+1D7F6 ACCEPT / 4301 REJECT.

ARBITRARY PRECISION: accepted values are exact Python ints with no 64-bit truncation. A 400-digit input prints all 400 digits verbatim in the output dict. A 4300-digit input prints all 4300 digits (verified digit run length == 4300). Because parsing caps at 4300 digits, the output side never trips the int-to-str limit.

MIXED SCRIPTS AND SIGNS: digits from different scripts may be freely mixed with each other, with ASCII digits and with underscores. Verified: '1'+U+0665 -> 15; U+0967+U+FF12+'3' -> 123; U+0E55+'_'+'7' -> 57; U+0665+'_'+U+FF17 -> 57. The sign, however, must be ASCII '+' or '-': U+2212 MINUS SIGN, U+FF0B FULLWIDTH PLUS and U+FF0D FULLWIDTH HYPHEN-MINUS are all REJECTED, while ASCII '-' + U+FF15 -> -5 and ASCII '+' + U+0665 -> 5.

NON-Nd NUMERICS ARE REJECTED even when they have a numeric value, because Step A only maps category Nd. Verified rejects: U+00B2 '²', U+00B9 '¹', U+00B3 '³', U+2070 '⁰', U+2074 '⁴', U+2460 '①', U+2164 'Ⅴ', U+216C 'Ⅼ', U+2185 'ↅ', U+3007 '〇', U+1369 '፩', U+0F2A '༪', U+00BD '½', U+2189 '↉', U+4E00 '一'.

OUTPUT FORMAT OF ACCEPTED VALUES: always rendered as a plain ASCII decimal Python int repr — optional leading '-', then digits, no '+', no leading zeros, no underscores, no thousands separators, and no trace of the original script. Verified: --b=U+0665 U+0666 and --c=U+FF17 produce `{'values_changed': {"root['y']": {'new_value': 7, 'old_value': 56}}}`; a full run with Unicode-digit args contains zero non-ASCII bytes on stdout. '-0' and '٥' style inputs normalise to `0` and `5`.

EXACT REJECT OUTPUT for an int() failure: stdout is EMPTY (0 bytes), exit code is 2, and stderr is exactly two LF-terminated lines:
line 1: `usage: test15_executable [-h] --a A --b B --c C\n`
line 2: `test15_executable: error: argument {OPT}: invalid int value: {REPR}\n`
where {OPT} is literally `--b` or `--c` and {REPR} is Python's `repr()` of the raw argv string. There is no truncation: a rejected 4301-digit value has its entire 4301-character repr in the message (4411 bytes of stderr).

EXACT REJECT OUTPUT for the argparse option-lookalike failure (Gate 1): same shape, exit 2, stdout empty, but line 2 is `test15_executable: error: argument {OPT}: expected one argument\n`. A wholly missing flag instead gives `test15_executable: error: the following arguments are required: --c`.

{REPR} FOLLOWS STANDARD PYTHON str.__repr__, NOT json-style escaping. Quote choice: single quotes by default; if the string contains `'` but no `"`, the whole thing is wrapped in double quotes with the apostrophe left bare; if it contains both, single quotes are used and `'` is escaped as `'`. Escapes: `\` for backslash, `
`, ``, `	`, and `\xNN` / `\uNNNN` / `\UNNNNNNNN` for codepoints where `str.isprintable()` is false. Printable non-ASCII codepoints are emitted as RAW UTF-8, not escaped (so this is ensure_ascii=False behaviour, unlike the Delta JSON). Verified: $'a
b' -> `'a
b'`; "it's" -> `"it's"`; `it'"s` -> `'it'"s'`; 'a ' -> `'a\b'`; $'ab' -> `'ab'`; U+007F -> `'\x7f'`; 'ü' -> raw bytes `c3 bc` inside single quotes; U+1F600 -> raw emoji `'\U0001f600'` rendered literally as 😀; U+0301 combining acute -> emitted raw; U+00A0 -> `'\xa0'`; U+3000 -> `'　'`; U+2028 -> `' '`; U+180E -> `'᠎'`; U+200B -> `'​'`; U+FEFF -> `'﻿'`; U+3164 (category Lo, printable) -> raw `'ㅤ'`.

rules: QUOTE SELECTION (R1): Let s be the string. Use `"` as the delimiter if and only if (s contains U+0027 APOSTROPHE) AND (s does NOT contain U+0022 QUOTATION MARK). In every other case (no apostrophe / apostrophe+quote both present / quote only / empty string) use `'` as the delimiter. Verified all 4 combos: `plain`->'plain'; `it's`->"it's"; `say "hi"`->'say "hi"'; `both ' and "`->'both \' and "'.

QUOTE ESCAPING (R2): Inside the body only two characters get a backslash-prefix escape: the chosen delimiter (emitted as backslash+delimiter) and U+005C REVERSE SOLIDUS (emitted as `\\`). The NON-chosen quote character is always emitted literally, never escaped. So `\'` can only ever appear when the string contains BOTH quote kinds; `\"` never appears in any output.

THREE SPECIAL CONTROL ESCAPES (R3): exactly three codepoints get letter escapes: U+0009 -> `\t`, U+000A -> `\n`, U+000D -> `\r`. No other letter escapes exist. There is NO `\a`, `\b`, `\f`, `\v`, `\0`, `\e` form in the output.

NUMERIC ESCAPE FORM (R4): every other non-printable codepoint c is emitted as: `\x` + 2 lowercase hex digits if c < 0x100; `\u` + 4 lowercase hex digits if 0x100 <= c < 0x10000; `\U` + 8 lowercase hex digits if c >= 0x10000. Always zero-padded to exactly 2/4/8 digits, hex letters ALWAYS lowercase (a-f). Verified exhaustively over all 1,112,064 non-surrogate codepoints U+0020..U+10FFFF: zero deviations from this form.
CONFIRMED NOT SPECIAL-CASED (R5): 0x07->`\x07`, 0x08->`\x08`, 0x0B->`\x0b`, 0x0C->`\x0c`, 0x1B->`\x1b`, 0x7F->`\x7f`. (Positive counterpart: 0x09/0x0A/0x0D DO get \t/\n/\r.)

ASCII MAP (R6), complete and exhaustively verified in one probe: 0x01-0x08 -> \x01..\x08; 0x09 -> \t; 0x0A -> \n; 0x0B -> \x0b; 0x0C -> \x0c; 0x0D -> \r; 0x0E-0x1F -> \x0e..\x1f; 0x20 (SPACE) -> literal space; 0x21-0x7E -> literal (with 0x22/0x27/0x5C subject to R1/R2); 0x7F -> \x7f.

NON-ASCII PRINTABILITY (R7): a codepoint is escaped iff str.isprintable() is false, i.e. iff its Unicode General_Category is one of Cc, Cf, Cs, Co, Cn, Zl, Zp, Zs — with U+0020 the single exception (Zs but printable). All other categories (including Mn combining marks) print literally as raw UTF-8. Positive (escaped) confirmations: U+00A0 Zs -> \xa0; U+00AD Cf -> \xad; U+0080..U+009F Cc -> \x80..\x9f; U+200B Cf -> ​; U+2028 Zl ->  ; U+2029 Zp ->  ; U+2000-U+200A Zs; U+202F, U+205F, U+1680, U+2007, U+180E, U+3000 Zs -> \uXXXX; U+2060, U+FEFF, U+200E Cf; U+E000-U+F8FF Co; U+0378, U+FFFF, U+FDD0-U+FDEF, U+1FFFE Cn. ASTRAL ESCAPE WIDTH (R4 confirmed for >=0x10000): U+E0001 Cn -> `\U000e0001`; U+1D173 Cf -> `\U0001d173`; U+10FFFF Cn -> `\U0010ffff`; U+100000 Co -> `\U00100000`; U+2EBF0 Cn -> `\U0002ebf0`. Negative: U+1F600 prints as raw 4-byte UTF-8 f0 9f 98 80, NOT \U0001f600.

UNICODE DATA VERSION (R8): the packed interpreter uses Unicode 15.0.0 (CPython 3.12). Fingerprint: U+1E030, U+1E06D, U+11F00, U+11F10, U+1E4D0, U+1DF25, U+10EFD, U+10EFF are PRINTABLE (assigned in 15.0); U+2FFC, U+31EF, U+2EBF0 are ESCAPED (assigned only in 15.1); U+105C0, U+10D40, U+11BC0, U+16D40, U+1E5D0, U+116D0, U+1CC00 are ESCAPED (assigned only in 16.0). An implementation must use a Unicode 15.0 category table, not the host's newest. The exhaustive observed non-printable set is 965,114 codepoints in 712 ranges, written to /tmp/reprarea/nonprintable_ranges.txt (format: space-separated uppercase-hex `AAAA` or `AAAA-BBBB`, inclusive, covers 0000-10FFFF including 0000-001F and D800-DFFF).

ARGV DECODING / SURROGATES (R9): argv bytes are decoded as UTF-8 with errors='surrogateescape'. Every byte B in 0x80..0xFF that is not part of a valid UTF-8 sequence becomes codepoint U+DC00+B, which is category Cs (non-printable, < 0x10000) and therefore renders as `\udcHH` with HH = lowercase hex of B. Exhaustively verified for all B in 0x80..0xFF (A\x80A\x81...A\xff produced \udc80..\udcff in order). Exit code is 0 and stdout stays well-formed. Over-long/illegal sequences are byte-wise escaped too: `\xc0\x80` -> `\udcc0\udcc0`... (actually `\udcc0\udc80`), UTF-8-encoded surrogate `\xed\xb2\x80` -> `\udced\udcb2\udc80`, out-of-range `\xf4\x90\x80\x80` -> `\udcf4\udc90\udc80\udc80`.

UNREACHABLE INPUTS (R10): U+0000 can never be delivered via argv (execve strings are NUL-terminated; bash also drops NUL from command substitution) — the byte is silently dropped, so `X\x00Y` yields `'XY'`. Lone surrogates other than U+DC80..U+DCFF are likewise unreachable. So `\x00` and `\ud800`-style output can never occur in practice.

STDOUT ENCODING (R11): stdout is UTF-8 regardless of environment. Printable non-ASCII codepoints are written as raw UTF-8 bytes (verified: U+1F600 -> f0 9f 98 80, U+00E9 -> c3 a9, U+4E2D -> e4 b8 ad). Setting LC_ALL=C, LC_ALL=C.utf8, PYTHONIOENCODING=ascii, or PYTHONUTF8=0 does NOT change the byte output at all (the PyInstaller bootloader pins it), so the implementation can hard-code UTF-8.

DICT REPR FORMAT (R12): `{` + `, `.join(repr(key) + `: ` + repr(value)) + `}` — one U+0020 after each `:`, `, ` (comma+space) between items, no space after `{` or before `}`. INT REPR (R13): ints are rendered with str(): plain decimal, `-` prefix for negatives, never `+`, never underscores, never thousands separators, `0` for zero. Verified: --b '+0007' -> 7; --b '  -1_000  ' -> -1000; --c 0 -> 0.
